design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) meta-analyses and GRADE ratings of randomized trials of cannabinoids against placebo, usual care or active drugs for ten indications prespecified by the funder, the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health: nausea and vomiting due to chemotherapy, appetite in HIV/AIDS, chronic pain, spasticity due to multiple sclerosis or paraplegia, depression, anxiety disorder, sleep disorder, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome. 79 trials (151 reports; 6462 participants), mostly of pharmaceutical cannabinoids (nabiximols, dronabinol, nabilone, THC); primary analyses used parallel-group trials only, with crossover trials in sensitivity analyses; short-term adverse events were pooled across all indications.
can_establish: The average short-term effects (follow-up mostly 2 to 15 weeks) of mostly pharmaceutical cannabinoids on symptoms, and their short-term adverse-event profile, in randomized trials of patients with the ten listed conditions published up to April 2015, with the review team's GRADE ratings of certainty.
cannot_establish: Long-term benefits or harms (no long-term studies were found); the effects of herbal cannabis as people use it outside trials (few trials tested smoked or vaporized cannabis, mostly crossover trials outside the primary analyses, at stated concentrations or potencies of 1.29% to 9.4%); effects against current standard treatments (most antiemetic comparators were older drugs); effects in people without the listed conditions; and anything about non-medical use.

sample.recruitment: Search of 28 databases and grey-literature sources from inception to April 2015, without language or date restrictions, with an information-specialist search strategy peer reviewed by a second specialist, screening of reference lists, and use of conference abstracts and trial-registry records as sources (Methods › Identification and Selection of Studies; Methods › Data Collection and Study Appraisal, 1st paragraph). Trial participants were patients with the listed conditions recruited by the primary trials; settings are described only in eAppendices 3 to 12 (not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized trials comparing cannabinoids with usual care, placebo or no treatment in the ten indications chosen by the funder. Nonrandomized studies, including case series of at least 25 patients, were eligible only where no randomized trial existed for an indication or outcome (for example long-term adverse events such as cancer, psychosis, depression or suicide); none was found for long-term adverse events (Methods › Study Eligibility Criteria; Results › Adverse Events). Depression and anxiety appear as indications, but no trial of depression treatment met the criteria, and the one anxiety trial tested a single dose in a simulated public-speaking test.
sample.demographics: Where reported, the proportion of men ranged from 0% to 100% (median 50%, 57 studies) and of white participants from 50% to 99% (median 78%, 18 studies); trials were published from 1975 to 2015 (median 2004; one third before 1990) in many countries (Results, 1st paragraph). Ages, previous cannabis experience and concomitant treatments are not reported in the main text.
sample.attrition: Within the trials, incomplete outcome data was the main source of bias: more than half reported substantial withdrawals not adequately handled in the analysis (Results, 2nd paragraph). Withdrawals due to adverse events were more frequent with cannabinoids (OR 2.94, Table 3).
sample.selection_effects: The indications were chosen by the funder, not by the reviewers, so conditions for which cannabis is widely used under state laws but which the funder did not list were not reviewed. The trial evidence is dominated by a few pharmaceutical products: nabiximols (19 placebo-controlled studies), dronabinol (10) and nabilone (7 placebo-controlled plus 13 against active drugs) in Table 1. Trials of plant material (2 rows labelled cannabis, 5 labelled smoked THC) were mostly crossover trials and so outside the primary analyses: in their reply to a letter (JAMA 2015;314:1751-1752) the authors state that 4 of the 5 smoked or inhaled cannabis trials from the University of California Center for Medicinal Cannabis Research were crossover trials. Nine trials were available only as abstracts and/or registry records.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment in randomized trials: dronabinol (synthetic THC, oral), nabilone (synthetic THC-like cannabinoid, oral), nabiximols (oromucosal spray with 27 mg THC and 25 mg CBD per mL), levonantradol (oral or intramuscular), THC capsules, THC oromucosal spray, smoked THC cigarettes, THC/CBD capsules, cannabidiol capsules or spray, ajulemic acid, ECP002A, and herbal cannabis smoked or vaporized (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: doses varied widely between and within products and were titrated in many trials (Table 1 gives the ranges tested). Routes: oral capsules or tablets, oromucosal spray, smoking, vaporizing, intramuscular injection. Plant material: two concentrations (1.29% and 3.53%) in the vaporized-cannabis trial, and potencies of 2.5% to 9.4%, where reported, in the smoked-THC cigarette trials. Follow-up in Table 2 ranged from 107 minutes (the single anxiety trial) to 15 weeks; most entries are 2 to 15 weeks. For each efficacy pool one arm per trial was used, the dose most similar to the other trials; for adverse events the highest dose was used, which the authors describe as a worst case (Discussion › Strengths and Weaknesses, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: participants' use of cannabis or other drugs outside the trials is not reported. Several trials tested cannabinoids added to existing treatment (for example in opioid-treated cancer pain, or with gabapentin, by their titles and the Chronic Pain section); the review does not distinguish add-on from stand-alone use.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Washout periods of the crossover trials are not described in the main text; the authors note that crossover trials risk unblinding through strong treatment effects or adverse events.

comparison.controls: Placebo in most trials. Active comparators mainly in the nausea-and-vomiting trials (prochlorperazine in 15 studies, 13 of them without a placebo arm, chlorpromazine 2, domperidone 2; alizapride, hydroxyzine, metoclopramide and ondansetron in single studies); also megestrol acetate (HIV), amitriptyline and dihydrocodeine (pain, sleep) and amisulpride (psychosis).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. Only 4 of 79 trials were at low risk of bias overall; 57% reported appropriate blinding of participants and 24% of outcome assessors (Results, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the observational sense (randomized comparisons). Not reported, and relevant to blinding and tolerability: participants' previous experience with cannabis. Functional unblinding of parallel-group trials by psychoactive effects is not discussed, although the review's own adverse-event data show strong excess euphoria (OR 4.08) and dizziness (OR 5.09).

outcomes.instruments: Nausea and vomiting: complete response. HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks, appetite, body fat. Pain: 30% or greater reduction on numerical rating (NRS) or visual analogue scales, NRS 0 to 10, Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form, Neuropathic Pain Scale (0 to 100), patient global impression of change, EQ-5D. Spasticity: Ashworth scale, NRS, 30% and 50% reductions on NRS, Barthel Index of activities of daily living, timed walking, global impression. Depression: Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Montgomery-Asberg scale, Beck Depression Inventory. Anxiety: Visual Analogue Mood Scale during a simulated public-speaking test. Sleep: Apnea-Hypopnea Index, insomnia and restfulness scores, sleep quality and disturbance NRS. Psychosis: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, PANSS. Glaucoma: intraocular pressure. Tourette syndrome: four tic-severity scales. Adverse events: any, serious, withdrawal due to adverse events, MedDRA high-level groupings and individual events (Table 2, Table 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Trials were rated with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (low only if all domains low, high if any domain high, otherwise unclear) by two reviewers independently; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE across risk of bias, publication bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness and magnitude of effect. Table 2's footnotes, printed on the table image, define the GRADE grades but give no reasons for individual ratings, so the downgrading decisions cannot be read.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: odds ratios for dichotomous outcomes and weighted mean differences for continuous outcomes, change from baseline where available and follow-up values otherwise, combined in the same pools as the Cochrane Handbook allows. No threshold of clinically important difference is stated for any continuous outcome. Harm: odds of experiencing each adverse event with the cannabinoid (highest dose) against placebo or active comparator, all indications combined.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 74 counts the 28 efficacy entries in Table 2 (16 pooled estimates and 12 single-trial results) and the 46 adverse-event estimates in Table 3; the text adds subgroup estimates (smoked THC, neuropathic and cancer pain).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening of records and full texts, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were each done by two reviewers independently, with a third resolving disagreements; GRADE assessments were made by one author (Article Information › Additional Author Contributions).

analysis.effect_sizes: All versus placebo unless stated; parallel-group trials only; random effects. Nausea and vomiting, complete response: OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42), 3 trials, 102 patients, I2=0%, GRADE low (abstract: 47% vs 20%). HIV weight gain: OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27), 1 trial, 88 patients, low. Chronic pain, 30% or greater reduction: OR 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), 8 trials (7 nabiximols, 1 smoked THC), 1370 patients, I2=48%, moderate (abstract: 37% vs 31%); NRS pain: WMD -0.46 points on 0 to 10 (-0.80 to -0.11), 6 trials, 948 patients, I2=59%, moderate; Brief Pain Inventory: -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16), 3 trials, moderate; Neuropathic Pain Scale: -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47), 5 trials, moderate; global impression of change: OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59), 6 trials, 267 patients, I2=68%, low; EQ-5D: -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02), 3 trials, moderate. Spasticity (multiple sclerosis): Ashworth WMD -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01), 5 trials, not significant (the overall as corrected in the abstract, also in Figure 3; Table 2 prints only per-product values, nabiximols -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02), 1244 patients by Table 2 (1134 by Figure 3's totals), I2=0%, moderate; NRS: -0.76 (-1.38 to -0.14), 3 trials, I2=73%, low; 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41) and 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83), 2 trials each, low; Barthel ADL: no pooled estimate, three per-product values (nabilone -0.58, -1.73 to 0.56; dronabinol 0.23, -0.13 to 0.59; THC/CBD -0.03, -0.39 to 0.33), moderate; walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36), 2 trials, moderate; global impression OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 3 trials, low. Sleep, trials in other indications: sleep quality WMD -0.58 (-0.87 to -0.29), 8 trials, very low; sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00), 3 trials, very low. Adverse events (highest dose; placebo or active comparators; all indications): any OR 3.03 (2.42 to 3.80), 29 studies, 3714 patients, I2=31%; serious 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92), 34 studies, 3248 patients, I2=0%; withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96), 23 studies; death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00), 5 studies. No tau-squared or prediction intervals; absolute numbers only as the abstract's two pairs of percentages and the event counts of Figures 2 (pain responders, 254/685 vs 215/685) and 4 (any adverse event, 1438/1779 vs 1058/1710).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable: randomized comparisons pooled as reported; heterogeneity examined by stratifying on cannabinoid, pain condition and, for any adverse event, meta-regression on cannabinoid, design, indication, comparator and duration of follow-up.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that they established a protocol, provided as eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 (not read), drafted by five of the authors; no registration (for example in PROSPERO) is reported. The indications were prespecified by the funder.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 reports parallel-group pools and primary outcomes only; the crossover sensitivity analyses are described as consistent with the primary analyses but their numbers are not in the main text. The abstract presents the pain responder result (OR 1.41, 0.99 to 2.00) and the Ashworth result (WMD -0.12, -0.24 to 0.01) among the associations found, although both intervals include no effect; the Results text says so for Ashworth only. Event proportions are given in the abstract, and event counts only in Figures 2 and 4.
analysis.power: Many indications rest on very small trials (glaucoma 6 participants, Tourette syndrome 17 to 18 per analysis, sleep apnea 22, anxiety 24, psychosis 35), which the authors say may have lacked power; pooled efficacy estimates draw on 2 to 8 trials each.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In short trials, mostly of nabiximols, dronabinol and nabilone, cannabinoids compared with placebo produced: a higher complete-response rate for chemotherapy nausea and vomiting in 3 small trials (OR 3.82, 1.55 to 9.42; 47% vs 20%); a borderline, non-significant increase in the proportion with at least 30% pain relief (OR 1.41, 0.99 to 2.00; 37% vs 31%, an absolute difference of about 6 percentage points, editors' arithmetic) and a reduction of under half a point on a 0 to 10 pain scale (-0.46); no significant change on the Ashworth spasticity scale (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01) and a 0.76-point reduction on numerical rating scales of spasticity; and small effects on sleep scores in pain and multiple-sclerosis trials. The odds of any adverse event were about three times higher (OR 3.03), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times higher, and of withdrawal because of adverse events about three times higher (OR 2.94); absolute numbers are given only as Figure 4's event counts for any adverse event (crude totals about 81% against 62%, editors' arithmetic). No long-term data exist. Evidence for depression, anxiety, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome comes from one or two small trials per indication.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the Conclusions say there was "moderate-quality evidence to support the use of cannabinoids" for chronic pain and spasticity. Gaps: (1) the outcomes rated moderate are either not statistically significant (30% pain relief, OR 1.41, 0.99 to 2.00; Ashworth -0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; Barthel, walking speed, EQ-5D) or small (NRS pain -0.46 of 10 points, against which no threshold of clinical importance is set), while the significant spasticity outcomes (numerical rating scales, global impression of change) are rated low; moderate certainty about a small or uncertain effect is not evidence that supports use, and the Discussion's own wording, that cannabinoids may be beneficial, is more guarded (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); (2) the evidence for pain and spasticity is mostly nabiximols, yet conclusions are drawn for cannabinoids in general, and the same-issue editorial reads the reviews as supporting marijuana (D'Souza and Ranganathan, JAMA 2015, first paragraph); (3) the Discussion calls the psychosis evidence low-quality evidence of no effect, but the only estimate compares cannabidiol with the antipsychotic amisulpride in 35 patients with a very wide interval, which cannot show absence of an effect; likewise for depression, where no treatment trial existed and the data are depressive symptoms in pain and multiple-sclerosis trials; (4) the conclusion lists weight gain in HIV and sleep disorders among low-quality evidence of improvement, but the only HIV estimate in Table 2 is a non-significant single trial (OR 2.2, 0.68 to 7.27), and the pooled sleep outcomes come from trials in other indications rated very low; (5) adverse events are summarized as an increased risk without absolute numbers, although Figure 4 shows any adverse event was common in both groups (crude totals 1438/1779 vs 1058/1710, about 81% vs 62%, editors' arithmetic). Against this, the review states its limitations plainly: most trials at high risk of bias, small samples, heterogeneous outcomes, no long-term data, and very little evidence on cannabis itself.

timeline.event: Earlier single-indication reviews cited in the Discussion (refs 167 to 196), for example the Cochrane review of cannabis and schizophrenia (Rathbone et al., 2008), the Cochrane review of cannabinoids for Tourette syndrome (Curtis et al., 2009), a meta-analysis of nabiximols for spasticity in multiple sclerosis (Wade et al., 2010) and a Cochrane review of neuromodulators for rheumatoid-arthritis pain (Richards et al., 2012), the only earlier review the authors found that used GRADE.

This review (June 2015), published with an editorial by D'Souza and Ranganathan (JAMA 2015;313:2431-2432, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.6407), whose openly visible first paragraph reads this review and a companion clinical review (Hill, JAMA 2015) as giving some evidence for marijuana in chemotherapy nausea, specific pain syndromes and multiple-sclerosis spasticity, and poor evidence for most other conditions qualifying under state laws. Only that paragraph was accessible.

Letters: Grant (JAMA 2015;314:1750-1751, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.11429), on the five placebo-controlled trials of smoked or inhaled cannabis for neuropathic pain run by the University of California Center for Medicinal Cannabis Research; Schatman (JAMA 2015;314:1751, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.11435), questioning moderate-quality evidence for pain and spasticity when preparations with different routes and pharmacodynamics were pooled. Reply by Whiting and Wolff (JAMA 2015;314:1751-1752, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.11447): all five trials were included, but four were crossover trials and so only in the sensitivity analyses. Only the first paragraph of each item was openly accessible.

Corrections, each confirmed in Crossref and read on the journal's page at adjudication: Figure 4's axis labels were swapped (JAMA 2015;314(5):520, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.8253; article corrected online 26 June 2015); the Ashworth estimate in the abstract should read WMD -0.12 (95% CI -0.24 to 0.01), 5 trials (JAMA 2015;314(8):837, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.9010; corrected online 13 July 2015); ajulemic acid's nonproprietary name (JBT-101, CT3) and US status (not currently in clinical use) in Table 1 (JAMA 2015;314(21):2308, doi 10.1001/jama.2015.15929; corrected online 5 November 2015).

Correction of the wording of the nabilone insomnia and sleep-restfulness estimates in the fifth sentence of the Sleep Disorder section (JAMA 2016;315(14):1522, doi 10.1001/jama.2016.3470; confirmed in Crossref and read at adjudication); the notice says the change does not affect the results.

replication.where_it_stands: The broadest review of randomized trials of medical cannabinoids up to April 2015 and widely cited for its conclusion on chronic pain and spasticity. The full text supports a narrower reading: short-term, small or uncertain benefits of mostly pharmaceutical cannabinoids, a clear excess of short-term adverse events, and no long-term evidence. The project holds the National Academies' 2017 report (nasem_2017), and the list for this page names later reviews (Stockings et al. 2018 and McDonagh et al. 2022 on chronic pain; Black et al. 2019 on mental-health conditions); none was read for this card, and claims about medical effectiveness should be checked against them.

funding.funder: Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH), grant agreement 14.001443/204.0001/-1257 (as printed: this funded by the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health). The FOPH prespecified the indications and, by the authors' statement, had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, preparation or approval of the manuscript or the decision to submit; publication was a condition of the funding, decided before any results were available. Dr Whiting's time was partly supported by the NIHR Collaboration for Leadership in Applied Health Research and Care West at University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE form and declare support from the FOPH for the submitted work, no financial relationships with any organizations that might have an interest in the submitted work in the previous 3 years, and no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced it. No additional disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Kleijnen Systematic Reviews Ltd (York), the University of Bristol and NIHR CLAHRC West, and from universities and hospitals in Italy, the Netherlands, Peru and the USA, and Cepicon GmbH (Hamburg). The review does not report or discuss who sponsored the included trials; in the reference list many trial-registry records, most of them of nabiximols (Sativex) or other cannabis-based medicine extracts, have GW Pharmaceuticals or GW Pharma Ltd as registrant (for example refs 19, 22, 23, 91, 104 to 109, 141 to 143).

what_would_settle_it: Large, parallel-group trials of defined cannabinoid products, including herbal cannabis at the potencies now sold, against current standard treatments as well as placebo, with checks of blinding, prespecified thresholds of clinically important change on patient-relevant outcomes, complete handling of withdrawals, follow-up of months rather than weeks, and systematic monitoring of long-term harms such as dependence and psychiatric and cognitive effects.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (patients with ten named conditions), intervention (cannabinoids), comparators (usual care, placebo, no treatment) and outcomes stated (Methods › Study Eligibility Criteria; Data Collection and Study Appraisal).
The authors state that they established a protocol and provide it as eAppendix 1 (not read; its contents and timing could not be checked); no registration is reported and no deviations are discussed.
Randomized trials for benefits, with nonrandomized studies of at least 25 patients admitted only where no trial existed for an indication or outcome, such as long-term adverse events.

28 databases and grey-literature sources, no language or date limits, peer-reviewed strategy (Embase strategy in eAppendix 2), reference lists screened, trial-registry records used, search within two months of publication. Of the criteria for 'yes', only consultation of content experts is not reported.
Search results and full texts were assessed independently by two reviewers, with consensus or a third reviewer.
Extraction and risk-of-bias assessment by two reviewers independently, with a third resolving disagreements.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article does not mention a list of excluded studies, and the publisher's list of the supplements' contents (protocol; search strategy; one appendix per indication; risk of bias of each included study; references) contains none. Figure 1 (flow diagram) could not be viewed; its footnote shows that excluded reports were counted at full-text stage.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: Table 1 summarizes interventions, routes, doses, comparators and numbers of studies by drug, but per-study populations, settings and follow-up are in eAppendices 3 to 12, which were not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for every trial (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting), by two reviewers; per-trial ratings in eAppendix 13, summary in the Results.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Trial sponsorship is not among the extracted items (baseline characteristics and outcomes) and is not reported or discussed, although manufacturer registrants are frequent in the reference list.

Random-effects pooling within groupings of indication, cannabinoid and outcome; one data set per trial to avoid double counting (one exception, Figure 3: a three-arm trial entered twice against its shared placebo group, with negligible weight); crossover trials, which none reported in a form allowing appropriate inclusion, kept out of the primary analyses; change-from-baseline and follow-up mean differences combined as the Cochrane Handbook permits.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses addressed trial design (crossover) only; no analysis by risk of bias, although 70% of trials were at high risk. GRADE downgrading is a judgment, not an analysis of impact on the estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Conclusions are graded with GRADE, which includes risk of bias, and the Discussion names the trials' weaknesses (withdrawals, selective reporting, randomization, concealment and blinding).

I2 is reported for each pool, analyses are stratified by cannabinoid and pain condition, adverse events were explored with meta-regression, and the heterogeneity of products, outcomes and time points is discussed (Discussion › Strengths and Weaknesses, 2nd paragraph).

No funnel plot or statistical test is described; publication bias is named only as a GRADE domain and as a reason for the broad search including unpublished trials, which reduces but does not investigate it.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funder, its role, and the authors' disclosures are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from eAppendices 3 to 12, which were not read; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Two critical items are not met (7, no list of excluded studies; 15, publication bias not investigated) and two are met only in part (2, protocol not registered; 4, no reported consultation of experts), so under the AMSTAR 2 rules confidence is critically low. The rating reflects those rules more than the conduct of the review, which is otherwise careful: a very broad search without language limits, registry and abstract sources, duplicate selection, extraction and risk-of-bias assessment, appropriate random-effects pooling and GRADE. For the encyclopedia the larger limitations lie in the evidence base the review describes: 55 of 79 trials at high risk of bias, mostly short trials of pharmaceutical products, very few trials of herbal cannabis in the primary analyses, and no long-term data. The review may be cited for the short-term effects and adverse events of cannabinoid medicines in trials, with the GRADE ratings attributed to the review team; it may not be cited for herbal or non-medical cannabis, for long-term harms, or as showing that cannabinoids have no effect on psychosis or depression.

key_findings.finding: Search and flow: 28 databases and grey-literature sources searched from inception to April 2015, no language or date restrictions; 23,754 records, 505 full texts, 79 trials (151 reports; 6462 participants) included, 3 of them in more than one indication; 34 parallel-group trials (4436 participants) and 45 crossover trials (2026); 4 trials available only as abstracts, 3 as abstracts with registry details, 2 only as registry records; trials published 1975 to 2015 (median 2004; one third before 1990).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Identification and Selection of Studies; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (Cochrane tool): 4 trials (5%) low, 55 (70%) high, 20 (25%) unclear. The main source was incomplete outcome data, with more than half of trials reporting substantial withdrawals not adequately handled; selective outcome reporting was a potential risk in 16%; 57% reported appropriate participant blinding and 24% appropriate outcome-assessor blinding.

Interventions (Table 1): nabiximols against placebo in 19 studies; dronabinol against placebo in 10; nabilone against placebo in 7 and against active drugs in 13; THC capsules, oromucosal spray (4 studies) and smoked THC cigarettes (5 studies; potency 2.5% to 9.4% where reported); herbal cannabis listed in 2 studies (vaporized at two concentrations, 1.29% and 3.53%, for pain; smoked for HIV); cannabidiol in 4; THC/CBD capsules in 4; levonantradol in 4; ajulemic acid and ECP002A in 1 each. The Discussion states that only 2 studies evaluated cannabis (refs 59 and 77) and found no evidence that its effects differed from other cannabinoids.
key_findings.note: Reference 77 (Abrams et al. 2007, a trial of cannabis by its title) is labelled smoked THC in the Results and Table 2, so the count of trials of plant material depends on the label (see reporting issues). Doses are study conditions.

key_findings.finding: Nausea and vomiting due to chemotherapy: 28 studies (37 reports; 1772 participants): 14 nabilone, 3 dronabinol, 1 nabiximols, 4 levonantradol, 6 THC; 8 placebo-controlled (3 with an active arm as well) and 20 against an active drug only; prochlorperazine was a comparator in 15 trials, 13 of the 20 active-only trials and 2 three-arm THC trials that also had placebo (editors' count from Table 1); risk of bias high in 23 and unclear in 5. Complete response, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) versus placebo: OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42), 3 trials, 102 patients, I2=0%, GRADE low; the abstract gives 47% versus 20%. No pooled comparison with active drugs is reported in the main text.
key_findings.locator: Results › Nausea and Vomiting Due to Chemotherapy; Table 2 (nausea and vomiting row); Abstract › Results

key_findings.finding: Appetite in HIV/AIDS: 4 studies (255 participants), all of dronabinol, all at high risk of bias; weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks, dronabinol versus placebo: OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27), 1 trial, 88 patients, GRADE low. In the one trial with a smoked-cannabis arm, both cannabis and dronabinol produced more weight gain than placebo; megestrol acetate produced more weight gain than dronabinol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Appetite Stimulation in HIV/AIDS Infection; Table 2 (HIV/AIDS row)

key_findings.finding: Chronic pain: 28 studies (63 reports; 2454 participants), mostly neuropathic pain (12) plus cancer pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, HIV neuropathy and others; 13 nabiximols, 4 smoked THC, 5 nabilone, 3 THC spray, 2 dronabinol, 1 vaporized cannabis, 1 ajulemic acid, 1 oral THC; all placebo-controlled except one against amitriptyline; risk of bias low in 2, unclear in 9, high in 17.
key_findings.note: The products listed sum to 30 for 28 studies; the text does not say which studies tested more than one.

key_findings.finding: Chronic pain, pooled versus placebo: 30% or greater pain reduction OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00), 8 trials, 1370 patients, I2=48%, GRADE moderate (abstract: 37% vs 31%); the one smoked-THC trial gave the largest effect, OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48), the other 7 were nabiximols; neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03), 6 trials. Nabiximols: NRS pain WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11) on a 0 to 10 scale, 6 trials, 948 patients, I2=59%, moderate; Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16), 3 trials; Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 (-7.32 to -0.47) on 0 to 100, 5 trials; global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59), 6 trials, 267 patients, I2=68%, low; EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02), 3 trials. Sensitivity analyses adding crossover trials were reported as consistent.
key_findings.locator: Results › Chronic Pain, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 (chronic pain rows); Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: The 30% responder estimate is not statistically significant (interval 0.99 to 2.00). The absolute difference implied by the abstract's percentages is about 6 percentage points (editors' arithmetic); how those percentages were derived is not described. The cancer-pain subgroup is printed with the same estimate and interval as the overall pool (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Spasticity: 14 studies (33 reports; 2280 participants), 11 in multiple sclerosis (2138) and 3 in paraplegia from spinal cord injury (142); all placebo-controlled; risk of bias low in 2, unclear in 5, high in 7; only multiple-sclerosis trials could be pooled. Ashworth scale WMD -0.12 (95% CI -0.24 to 0.01), 5 trials, not significant (1244 patients, I2=0%, GRADE moderate); spasticity NRS -0.76 (-1.38 to -0.14), 3 trials, 698 patients, I2=73%, low; 50% NRS reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41) and 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83), 2 trials each, low; Barthel ADL, 4 trials (1433 patients), moderate, favouring placebo: no pooled estimate, Table 2 printing three per-product values, -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56) beside Nabilone (2), 0.23 (-0.13 to 0.59) beside Dronabinol (1) and -0.03 (-0.39 to 0.33) beside THC/CBD (1), all including no difference; walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36), 2 trials, moderate; global impression OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 3 trials, 461 patients, low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Spasticity Due to MS or Paraplegia; Table 2 (spasticity rows); Figure 3; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: The Ashworth value is the overall as corrected in the abstract (correction notice doi 10.1001/jama.2015.9010, JAMA 2015;314(8):837, confirmed in Crossref and read at adjudication), also printed in the text and Figure 3. Table 2 prints no overall for this row: its three values are the per-product estimates of Figure 3 (nabiximols subtotal -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02, 4 trials, 383 vs 337 patients; THC/CBD -0.32, -1.59 to 0.95; dronabinol -0.94, -2.37 to 0.49, the last two the two arms of Zajicek 2003 against one placebo group of 207). Figure 3's totals are 590 and 544 patients (1134), against 1244 in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Depression, anxiety and psychosis: no trial of depression treatment qualified; 5 trials in other indications reported depression outcomes (2 unclear, 3 high risk of bias), 3 showing no difference, and one graded-dose trial in cancer pain showing worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (mean difference 2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses; single-trial estimates in Table 2 are all non-significant (HADS 0.15, MADRS 1.90, BDI 0.69), GRADE very low. Anxiety: one trial (24 patients, high risk of bias) of cannabidiol in social anxiety disorder, anxiety factor -16.52 (P=.01) during a simulated public-speaking test, follow-up 107 minutes, very low. Psychosis: 2 trials (71 participants), high risk of bias, cannabidiol against amisulpride or placebo, no difference; Table 2 gives cannabidiol versus amisulpride (35 patients) BPRS -0.10 (-9.20 to 8.90) and PANSS 1 (-12.60 to 14.60), GRADE low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Depression; Results › Anxiety Disorder; Results › Psychosis; Table 2 (depression, anxiety disorder and psychosis rows)

key_findings.finding: Sleep: 2 trials (5 reports; 54 participants) specifically for sleep problems: a parallel trial at high risk of bias reported an Apnea-Hypopnea Index difference of -19.64 (P=.02; 22 patients, GRADE low), and a crossover trial at low risk of bias in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24) and restfulness (0.48, 0.01 to 0.95). In 19 placebo-controlled trials for other indications (chronic pain, multiple sclerosis), mainly nabiximols: sleep quality WMD -0.58 (-0.87 to -0.29) on a 0 to 10 scale, 8 trials, I2 33%, and sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00), 3 trials, I2 64%, both favouring the cannabis-based medicine in Table 2's Favors column and both GRADE very low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sleep Disorder; Table 2 (sleep disorder rows)
key_findings.note: The insomnia and restfulness sentence is the corrected one: the journal's notice of 12 April 2016 (JAMA 2016;315(14):1522, doi 10.1001/jama.2016.3470, confirmed in Crossref and read at adjudication) gives the wording, nabilone being associated with improvements in insomnia and greater restfulness than amitriptyline, and says the change does not affect the results. The text and Table 2 attribute the apnea result to nabilone, but the reference list suggests a dronabinol trial (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 participants (unclear risk of bias) found no difference between THC or cannabidiol oromucosal spray and placebo in intraocular pressure. Tourette syndrome: 2 small placebo-controlled trials (4 reports; 36 participants) of THC capsules suggested less tic severity; Table 2 single-trial differences on four scales, 17 or 18 patients each (P=.03, P<.05, P=.061, P=.008), GRADE low.
key_findings.locator: Results › Glaucoma; Results › Movement Disorders Due to Tourette Syndrome; Table 2 (Tourette syndrome rows)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: reported in 62 studies (127 reports); meta-regression and stratified analyses found no difference in the association with any adverse event by cannabinoid, design, indication, comparator or duration, so all studies were combined (highest dose; placebo or active comparator). Any adverse event OR 3.03 (2.42 to 3.80), 29 studies, 3714 patients, I2=31%; serious adverse events 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92), 34 studies, 3248 patients, I2=0%; withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96), 23 studies, 2755 patients; death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00), 5 studies, 929 patients; psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29), 8 studies; nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58), 10 studies. No study of long-term adverse events was found, even among lower levels of evidence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events; Table 3 (general and MedDRA rows)

key_findings.finding: Individual adverse events, cannabinoid versus control: dizziness OR 5.09 (4.10 to 6.32), 41 studies; dry mouth 3.50 (2.58 to 4.75), 36; nausea 2.08 (1.63 to 2.65), 30; fatigue 2.00 (1.54 to 2.62), 20; somnolence 2.83 (2.05 to 3.91), 26; euphoria 4.08 (2.18 to 7.64), 27; vomiting 1.67 (1.13 to 2.47), 17; diarrhoea 1.65 (1.04 to 2.62), 17; disorientation 5.41 (2.61 to 11.19), 12; asthenia 2.03 (1.35 to 3.06), 15; drowsiness 3.68 (2.24 to 6.01), 18; confusion 4.03 (2.05 to 7.97), 13; loss of balance 2.62 (1.12 to 6.13), 6; hallucination 2.19 (1.02 to 4.68), 10 studies, 898 patients. Not significant: depression 1.32 (0.87 to 2.01), anxiety 1.98 (0.73 to 5.35), paranoia 2.05 (0.42 to 10.10), psychosis 1.09 (0.07 to 16.35, 2 studies, 37 patients), seizures 0.91 (0.05 to 15.66), dyspnoea 0.83 (0.26 to 2.63).
key_findings.note: Odds ratios, not risks: absolute frequencies are not reported, and for common events an odds ratio overstates the relative risk.

key_findings.finding: Synthesis methods: studies grouped by indication, cannabinoid and outcome and pooled with random effects where two or more trials were available; one data set per trial (the dose most similar to the other trials; for adverse events the highest dose); change-from-baseline mean differences preferred, follow-up differences otherwise; primary efficacy analyses restricted to parallel-group trials because no crossover trial reported data allowing appropriate inclusion, while adverse-event data from all conditions and both designs were combined, with design tested in meta-regression; heterogeneity examined with forest plots and I2; GRADE for certainty.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Synthesis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Strengths and Weaknesses, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 3 shows one departure from the one-data-set rule: Zajicek 2003 enters the Ashworth pool twice (dronabinol and THC/CBD arms against the same 207 placebo patients; weights 0.75% and 0.95%), with a negligible effect on the estimate. Figure 4 includes crossover trials (for example the 6-person glaucoma trial).

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain and spasticity; low-quality evidence suggests improvement in chemotherapy nausea and vomiting, weight gain in HIV, sleep disorders and Tourette syndrome; cannabinoids increase the risk of short-term adverse events. The Discussion adds very low-quality evidence of improved anxiety in a public-speaking test, low-quality evidence of no effect on psychosis and very low-quality evidence of no effect on depression, and calls for large robust trials, more trials of cannabis itself and standardized outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Unanswered Questions and Future Research; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Pain responders, per trial (Figure 2): 254 of 685 people with cannabinoids and 215 of 685 with placebo had at least 30% less pain across the 8 trials (37.1% and 31.4%, the abstract's 37% and 31%; editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), I2 47.6%; smoked THC (Abrams 2007) 13 of 25 against 6 of 25, OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48); the 7 nabiximols trials together 241 of 660 against 209 of 660, OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), I2 44.5%. Five trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly) and 3 favour placebo (none significantly).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (forest plot, 30% or greater pain reduction)
key_findings.note: Viewed on screen at adjudication (2026-10-31). The editors' random-effects recomputation from these counts reproduces the overall, nabiximols and neuropathic estimates.

key_findings.finding: Any adverse event, per trial (Figure 4): 29 trials, by cannabinoid; totals 1438 of 1779 people with cannabinoids and 1058 of 1710 with comparators (80.8% and 61.9%, editors' arithmetic; 3489 patients, against 3714 in Table 3), OR 3.03 (2.42 to 3.80), I2 31.2%; nabiximols subtotal 931 of 1101 against 727 of 1041, OR 2.41 (1.91 to 3.05). The comparator column is headed placebo but includes active-comparator antiemetic trials, and crossover trials are included.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4 (forest plot, any adverse event; axis labels as corrected on 26 June 2015)
key_findings.note: Viewed on screen at adjudication. These are the only absolute numbers for adverse events in the article; with events this common, the odds ratio of 3.03 corresponds to a crude ratio of proportions of about 1.3 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints no overall estimate for the Ashworth row: its three unlabelled values (-0.11, -0.23 to 0.02; -0.32, -1.59 to 0.95; -0.94, -2.37 to 0.49) are, as Figure 3 shows, the per-product estimates for nabiximols (subtotal of 4 trials), THC/CBD and dronabinol, the last two the two arms of Zajicek 2003. The overall -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01), the value given in the correction of 13 July 2015, is printed in the abstract, the text and Figure 3. The Barthel row has the same layout (-0.58, -1.73 to 0.56; 0.23, -0.13 to 0.59; -0.03, -0.39 to 0.33 beside Nabilone (2), Dronabinol (1), THC/CBD (1)) and no pooled estimate. Table 2's footnotes, printed on the table image, do not explain the cells.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (spasticity rows); Figure 3; Abstract › Results; Results › Spasticity Due to MS or Paraplegia
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the Ashworth overall as -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01) and say it is not significant. -0.58 must not be cited as a pooled 4-trial Barthel estimate: no Barthel pool is reported, and the per-product values may be cited only as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The cancer-pain subgroup of the 30% pain-reduction analysis is printed as OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00) from 2 trials, identical to the overall estimate from 8 trials.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Chronic Pain, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Almost certainly a copying error: the counts in Figure 2 for the two cancer-pain trials (Johnson 2010, Portenoy 2012) give OR 1.55 (0.51 to 4.70), I2 77% (editors' random-effects recomputation, matching the second reader's); the printed figure must not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The count of trials of plant material is inconsistent: the Discussion says only 2 studies evaluated cannabis (refs 59 and 77), Table 1 lists 2 cannabis studies (vaporized, smoked) and 5 smoked-THC cigarette studies with stated potencies, and the Results and Table 2 call ref 77 (Abrams et al. 2007, titled as a cannabis trial) smoked THC; the Chronic Pain section counts 4 smoked-THC studies and 1 vaporized-cannabis study.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Results › Chronic Pain, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; reference 77
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must not say that two trials tested cannabis; between 2 and 7 trials tested smoked or vaporized plant material, depending on labels, and only one of them (ref 77) is in the primary pain pool.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Table 2 attribute the parallel-group sleep-apnea trial (Apnea-Hypopnea Index -19.64, 22 patients) to nabilone, but the only sleep-apnea trial in the reference list is of dronabinol (ref 18, Prasad et al. 2011, an abstract), and the five reports of the two sleep trials match that abstract plus four reports of the nabilone fibromyalgia trial (refs 63, 64, 89, 90); Table 1 also lists sleep among dronabinol's indications.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Sleep Disorder; Table 2 (sleep disorder row); Table 1; references 18, 63, 64, 89, 90
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a mislabelled drug (editors' inference from the reference list); the apnea result should not be cited as a nabilone effect.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3, renal and urinary disorders are given as OR 2.45 (95% CI 2.27 to 2.65) from 3 studies with 470 patients. An interval this narrow implies a standard error of the log odds ratio of about 0.04, which would need many thousands of events; with 470 patients the smallest possible standard error is about 0.18 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (renal and urinary disorders row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval, and probably the estimate, is wrong; this row must not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Chronic Pain section the products tested sum to 30 (13 nabiximols, 4 smoked THC, 5 nabilone, 3 THC spray, 2 dronabinol, 1 vaporized cannabis, 1 ajulemic acid, 1 oral THC) for 28 studies; in Table 2 the Barthel ADL pool lists 2 nabilone trials although the Spasticity section counts only 1 nabilone study, and the Ashworth pool lists 6 product-trials (4 nabiximols, 1 THC/CBD, 1 dronabinol) for 5 trials.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Chronic Pain, 1st paragraph; Results › Spasticity Due to MS or Paraplegia; Table 2 (spasticity rows)
reporting_issues.consequence: For the Ashworth pool Figure 3 gives the reason: one three-arm trial (Zajicek 2003) enters as two comparisons, dronabinol and THC/CBD, sharing its placebo group of 207, against the review's stated one-data-set rule (combined weight 1.7%; negligible effect on the estimate). The chronic-pain (30 products for 28 studies) and Barthel (2 nabilone trials against 1 nabilone study) counts remain unexplained; product-specific statements drawn from these pools are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentages in the abstract (complete nausea-and-vomiting response 47% vs 20%; pain reduction 37% vs 31%) appear nowhere in the Results text or tables, and their derivation is not described in words. For pain, Figure 2's event totals give them (254/685 = 37.1%, 215/685 = 31.4%: crude totals across trials); the nausea pool has no forest plot, so 47% vs 20% cannot be traced.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims using them must call the pain figures crude totals across trials and the nausea figures percentages given only in the abstract, not pooled risks.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's footnotes are not rendered in the HTML text but are printed on the table image (abbreviations, including CBM, cannabis based medicine; a, glaucoma; b, what the outcome cell contains, follow-up not shown for all studies; c, definitions of the GRADE grades); they give no reasons for individual GRADE ratings. The Results first place eAppendices 3 to 12 in Supplement 1 and later in Supplement 2; the publisher's list of supplements puts them in Supplement 2.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2; Supplemental Content list
reporting_issues.consequence: The reasons for each GRADE rating cannot be read from the article, in the HTML text or on the table image; claims should cite the GRADE ratings as the review team's judgments without their stated reasons.

reporting_issues.issue: Scale labels in Table 2 do not match the values or the text: the EQ-5D is labelled 0 to 100 while the pooled difference is -0.01 and the text calls it the EQ-5D health status index; the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale is labelled 0 to 52.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (chronic pain, quality-of-life row; depression row); Results › Chronic Pain, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the EQ-5D result is null on either scale, but its units should not be quoted from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 prints the heterogeneity P values as .94 (nabiximols subtotal, I2 44.5%, 6 df) and .64 (overall, I2 47.6%, 7 df); from the printed I2 values the Q statistics are about 10.8 and 13.4, giving P of about .094 and .064 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably dropped zeros; the I2 values and pooled estimates are unaffected, but the printed P values must not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Patient totals differ between figures and tables: Figure 3's overall Ashworth row counts 590 and 544 patients (1134) against 1244 in Table 2; Figure 4's any-adverse-event totals are 1779 and 1710 (3489) against 3714 in Table 3 for the same 29 studies.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Figure 3; Figure 4; Table 2 (Ashworth row); Table 3 (Any row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Unexplained; cite the table's patient numbers with the figure's beside them where it matters, and use the figure counts only as crude totals.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the sleep-quality pool as 8 trials with 539 patients and the sleep-disturbance pool as 3 trials with 1637 patients; for 3 trials against 8 these counts look transposed or wrong.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the patient counts of the two sleep pools should not be cited.
